youtube.title: How Starlink Internet Works (Why It's Faster Than Old Satellites)
youtube.summary: Starlink beams internet from space to a small flat dish. In this video we follow your data from the dish to a satellite and back, see why flying 550 km up instead of 35,786 km makes such a difference, how a dish with no moving parts follows satellites, how lasers pass data through space, and what can still slow it down.
youtube.details:
Key facts (checked November 2026):
- Starlink's main shell orbits at about 550 km; geostationary satellites sit at 35,786 km, roughly 65 times higher (EarthSims, updated Aug 2026)
- Geostationary round-trip delay is 600 ms or more; Starlink's real-world latency is typically about 20-50 ms (EarthSims)
- More than 6,000 satellites launched by early 2026; typical speeds 50-250 Mbps (EarthSims)
- The dish is a phased-array antenna that steers its beam electronically; it hands off to a new satellite roughly every 15-30 seconds (EarthSims)
- Newer satellites use laser inter-satellite links; ground stations (gateways) connect to the fibre internet (EarthSims)
- Light travels about 47% faster in vacuum than in glass fibre (refractive index of about 1.47)

shorts.headline: Why Starlink is faster than old satellites
A dish with no moving parts

scenes.sub: roughly 65 times closer than old internet satellites
scenes.text: Right now, thousands of small satellites are racing around the Earth, and some of them are carrying the internet to people who have never had a cable. This is Starlink. Its satellites orbit about five hundred and fifty kilometres above you. That is roughly sixty five times closer than the old internet satellites. And closer means faster. In this video we will follow your data from a small dish on the ground, up to a satellite, and back down again. We will see why the dish has no moving parts, how it switches satellites every few seconds, and what can still slow it down.

items.text: A round trip takes about 600 ms

scenes.text: To see why Starlink is different, look at the old way. Traditional internet satellites sit in a very high orbit, about thirty five thousand, seven hundred and eighty six kilometres up. At that height a satellite appears to hover over one spot, which is useful, but the distance is huge. A signal has to travel all the way up and all the way back down, and then do the same for the reply. That round trip takes around six hundred milliseconds at the very least. You notice that delay in video calls, in online games, and even when you simply load a web page.

Starlink solves this by flying much lower. Old satellites sit at thirty five thousand kilometres. Starlink's main group flies at about five hundred and fifty, which is called low earth orbit. The signal has far less distance to travel, so in everyday use the delay is often around twenty to fifty milliseconds, instead of six hundred or more. But there is a catch. A satellite that low can only see a small patch of ground, so one is not enough. Starlink needs a whole network working like a relay team. More than six thousand have been launched, and thousands are working in orbit at any moment.

items.text: Your dish sends the request up
A satellite passes it to a ground station
Fibre carries it to the website
The answer returns the same way

scenes.text: So what happens when you open a web page? First, a small dish at your home sends your request up to a satellite passing overhead, using radio waves. The satellite does not keep the data. It sends it down to a ground station, a large antenna site connected to the normal internet by fibre cables. From there, your request goes to the website, and the answer returns along the same path in reverse: ground station, satellite, and finally your dish. All of this usually happens in a fraction of a second, so it feels no different from any other connection.

scenes.chapterTitle: A dish with no moving parts
scenes.text: The dish is more clever than it looks. It is called a phased array antenna. Instead of one big dish that has to turn to follow a satellite, it has many tiny antennas on a flat panel. By timing the signal from each tiny antenna very slightly differently, the dish can aim its beam electronically, without moving at all. It can follow a satellite across the sky and even switch to another one, just by changing the timing. Small motors are used only once, during setup, to point the dish at a clear piece of sky. After that, it quietly does everything with electronics.

There is one more problem. Satellites that low move fast. A single satellite crosses your patch of sky in only a few minutes. So your dish cannot rely on one satellite. At any moment, a few satellites are visible, and your dish keeps switching to the best one, as often as every fifteen to thirty seconds. This handoff happens automatically, in the background. Software tracks where every satellite is, and tells each dish which one to talk to next. It is a bit like your phone moving from one mobile tower to the next while you drive, except that here the towers are the ones moving.

items.text: Data hops from satellite to satellite
It lands at a distant ground station

scenes.text: What about places with no ground station nearby, like the middle of an ocean? Newer Starlink satellites carry lasers. They use beams of light to send data directly from one satellite to the next, high above the Earth, in the vacuum of space. The data can hop across several satellites before it comes down at a ground station, possibly on another continent. Light travels about one and a half times faster in space than inside a glass fibre cable, which can make some long routes quicker. It also means ships, planes and remote islands can get online far from any cable or tower.

Those ground stations are called gateways. There are hundreds of them around the world, each with several large antennas, and each connected to the regular internet by fibre. Where gateways are close together, such as North America and Western Europe, the delay can be as low as twenty to thirty five milliseconds. In remote areas, with fewer gateways, the data may travel further, and the delay can climb to forty or sixty. So Starlink is not a replacement for the whole internet. It is a fast bridge that reaches the internet's cables from places where cables cannot reach.

items.name: Trees and buildings
items.desc: Block the view of the sky

scenes.text: Starlink is impressive, but it is not perfect. The dish needs a clear view of the sky, so tall trees and buildings can block the signal. Very heavy rain or snow can weaken it. And the capacity of each satellite is shared. If many people in the same area are online at the same time, speeds can drop at busy hours. Typical speeds are somewhere between fifty and two hundred and fifty megabits per second, which is fast, but it varies a lot from place to place and from day to day.

items.text: Ships and planes far from land

scenes.text: So why does this matter? For many people, the problem was never speed. It was simply that no company would lay cables to their village, farm or island. A dish and a clear sky can change that in an afternoon. Ships and planes can stay connected far from land. And when a storm or earthquake knocks down mobile towers, a dish can still reach a satellite overhead. Of course, there are open questions too, such as how crowded space is becoming. Astronomers also worry about bright satellites crossing their images. The technology is helpful, but it needs care.

items.text: Low orbit means a short, fast trip
A flat dish steers its beam, no motors
Lasers and ground stations join the internet

scenes.text: Let us recap in three points. One. Starlink satellites fly low, about five hundred and fifty kilometres up, so signals travel a short distance and the delay is small. Two. Your dish uses many tiny antennas to steer its beam electronically, and it switches between moving satellites every few seconds. Three. Data hops between satellites by lasers, lands at a ground station, and joins the normal internet. It is not magic from the sky. It is a very clever relay race.

scenes.title: How Starlink works
scenes.text: So the next time you see a line of lights crossing the night sky shortly after a launch, it might be a group of Starlink satellites, on their way to relay someone's video call. Now I want to hear from you. Would you ever use satellite internet at home? Tell me in the comments. If you enjoyed this, subscribe to Tech Explained. In the next video, we will find out how a QR code can store a web address in a pattern of tiny black and white squares.
